title.en: Li Ji, the Girl Who Volunteered to Slay the Serpent

region.en: Dongyue, the Peak of the East (Fujian, snake country)

texts.period: Soushen Ji (In Search of the Supernatural) by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 19

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 19: the great serpent of Yong ridges, the yearly maiden, and Li Ji

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: An eight-zhang serpent in the eastern hills demanded a maiden of twelve or thirteen every August, and the officials, offering slaves and land, sent nine girls to their deaths. Li Ji, the sixth daughter of a poor clerk, volunteered against her parents' weeping: she took a sword and a snake-sniffing hound, loaded rice-balls with honeyed sesame, and in the mouth of the cave baited, killed and beheaded the serpent — and found in its lair the skulls of the nine before her, saying as she came out that the timid ones had deserved their deaths.
summary.zh: 東越閩中庸嶺大蛇長八丈，歲八月輒送十二三歲女充祭，已食九女；將樂縣李誕家六女李寄自請應募——囓犬、斫密劍、蜜麨數石；蛇出食犬，寄以劍砍之——得九女髑髏，歎曰『汝曹怯弱，為蛇所食』，遂緩步而歸。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original.

passages.text: In the eastern land of Dongyue a serpent lay coiled in the hills, eighty feet long, that had once shown itself to the town and eaten the girls sent to charm it: every August the officers bought or seized a girl of twelve or thirteen, shut her in a chamber by the serpent's cave-mouth, and let the beast take her. Nine girls had gone to the chamber; the town went on sending.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 19, Li Ji episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Li Ji, sixth daughter of a poor clerk, offered herself against her parents' tears, took the reward of slaves and grain for her family, and prepared her own equipment: a sharp sword, a hound that loved to kill snakes, and several bushels of rice-balls kneaded with honeyed sesame. She set the sweet rice at the cave-mouth and waited with the hound behind her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 19, the preparations; not verbatim.

passages.text: The serpent came out, boiling with the sweetness, and plunged its head into the rice; the hound fastened on its throat, and Li Ji hacked at the wound until the beast died. In the lair she found the skulls of the nine maidens before her, and said to them, coming out unhurried: 'You were too soft to save yourselves.' She went home a heroine, and was married to the king of Yue.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 19, the killing and the skulls; not verbatim.

title.en: The Swords of Gan Jiang and Mo Ye, and the Head in the Cauldron

region.en: The Chu court and the southern mountains (pin: Hubei)

texts.period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 11 (older tellings in Lüshi Chunqiu and Wuyue Chunqiu)

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 11: the sword-smith's three years, the male sword in the pillar, and the boy's head boiled in the cauldron

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The sword-smith Gan Jiang forged a pair of swords for the king of Chu; three years in the furnace, the king killed him in anger — but the smith had hidden the male sword in a pillar and told his unborn son. The boy Mei-jian-chi grew, learned the riddle, dug out the sword, and met a stranger who offered to avenge him if he would give up his head and sword; the head, boiled in a cauldron, leapt a thousand times and would not scald, and the stranger cut off his own head to join it — three heads in one cauldron, buried together as the Tomb of the Three Kings.
summary.zh: 干將為楚王作劍三年乃成，王怒殺之；留雄劍於柱中，囑子出而取之。子赤比（眉間尺）得劍，遇客願為報仇，索頭與劍；頭鑊中三日照不爛，客自刎以頭助之——三首俱爛，合葬一處，是為三王墓。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original.

passages.text: Gan Jiang and his wife Mo Ye forged swords for the king of Chu; the metal was of such temper that the furnace took three years. When the king came in anger to demand them, the smith showed him only the female sword, and died by his blade — but he had hidden the male sword inside a pillar of the gate-tower, and told his pregnant wife: 'If the child is a boy, tell him to come out of the south gate, look at the pillar of the north hill, and find the sword in the wood.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 11, Gan Jiang episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy grew up asking about his father, learned the riddle, split the pillar and took the sword. The king dreamed of a boy with a brow like an inch-wide measure, and set a price on his head; the boy fled to the hills, singing his grief — until a stranger asked his story, and offered to do the vengeance if the boy would give him his head and the sword.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 11, Mei Jianchi episode; not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy cut off his own head and stood holding it and the sword, waiting for the promise; the stranger took both and went to the king, presenting the head in a cauldron of boiling water. Three days it boiled and would not scald; the head glared from the water. 'This head will not melt,' said the stranger, 'look closer' — and when the king bent over the cauldron, the stranger cut off the king's head, then his own, and all three heads boiled together. The courtiers buried the three in one mound, and the Tomb of the Three Kings stood in Yichun to be seen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 11, the cauldron and the tomb; not verbatim.

title.en: Han Ping and His Wife: The Mandarin Ducks of Kangle

texts.period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 11

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 11: the wife taken by the king, the double suicide, and the trees that grew together

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: King Kang of Song coveted the wife of his gate-clerk Han Ping, seized her, and sent Han Ping to hard labor; the wife sent him a coded letter of garters, the king laughed, and both took their lives — she jumped from the terrace, he hanged himself. The king buried them apart, saying they could not join in death if they had loved in life; in ten days two trees grew from the graves, curved toward each other, entwined their roots and branches — and mandarin ducks nested in the canopy, crying day and night.
summary.zh: 宋康王舍人韓憑妻何氏美，王奪之，罰憑築城；妻陰遺書，『其雨淫淫，河大水深，日出當心』——夫婦相繼自殺；王使冢分埋之，兩墳各生梓木，屈體相就，根交於下、枝錯於上；鴛鴦恆棲樹上，晨夕不去——宋人哀之，號其木曰相思樹。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original. Aition of the 'lovers' tree' (xiangsi shu) and of mandarin-duck symbolism for wedded fidelity.

passages.text: The wife of Han Ping, a clerk in the court of Song, was so beautiful that King Kang took her for himself and sent Han Ping to a chain-gang by the Great Wall. The wife sent her husband a letter in three riddling lines — rain that falls and falls, a river too deep to measure, the sun rising on a set heart — and both king and court read it and laughed, for only the husband knew it said: the king has me, the way is far, and I will die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 11, Han Ping episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Han Ping hanged himself in the laborers' camp. His wife, walking the king's terrace, had her robes lined with paper: she leapt from the height, her dress burst open in the air like a butterfly's wings, and the king, striking at the falling paper, could not save her. In her girdle was a plea: to be buried with her husband in one grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 11, the two deaths; not verbatim.

passages.text: The king buried the lovers apart, in plots within sight of each other, saying the dead could not undo his taking. In ten days a catalpa tree grew from each grave, bending toward the other until the roots met beneath the earth and the branches crossed in the air; and mandarin ducks came and nested in the canopy, crying to each other night and morning. The people of Song named the trees the Trees of Longing, and the terrace the Terrace of the Loving Couple.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 11, the entwined trees; not verbatim.

title.en: Dong Yong Sells Himself to Bury His Father, and a Weaver Girl Comes Down
title.zh: 董永賣身葬父織女相助

texts.period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 1 (Han iconography of Wuliang shrine, 2nd c. CE)

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 1: Dong Yong's sale of himself, the ten-day cloth, and the weaving-girl who descended for ten days

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Dong Yong, too poor to bury his dead father, sold himself into servitude for the funeral money and walked to the master's house to work it off. On the road a girl met him and asked to be his wife; in the master's house she wove in ten days a hundred bolts of cloth that should have taken a year — then told him, rising into the air: 'I am one of the Weaving Maidens of heaven; the Emperor of Heaven, moved by your filial piety, sent me to pay your debt.' And she was gone.
summary.zh: 董永喪父貧，賣身以葬；道遇一女求為妻，織縑百匹十日而畢——女凌空而去，曰『我天上織女，天帝感君孝，命我助君償債』——漢畫像石已見此圖。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original. The Cowherd-Weaver cycle's ethical core (filial piety rewarded) is anachronistic with the later love-tragedy version; both strands recorded.

passages.text: Dong Yong of Qiancheng was so poor at his father's death that he could not afford a coffin; he sold himself to a rich household for ten thousand cash, to be worked off as a servant, and walked to the master's house with the funeral done.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 1, Dong Yong episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the road a girl met him, saying she wished to be his wife; the master was told and agreed to set her to weaving, and the girl sat at the loom for ten days and wove a hundred bolts of fine cloth — the full price of the bond — and the debt was paid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 1, the weaving; not verbatim.

passages.text: The girl left the loom, rose into the air before him, and said: 'I am one of the Weaving Maidens of heaven. The Emperor of Heaven was moved by your filial piety, and sent me down for ten days to clear your debt.' And she was gone — the first telling of the heaven-sent weaver whose ten days of cloth redeemed a bondsman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 1, the ascent; not verbatim.

title.en: The Girl Who Was Wrapt in the Horse's Hide: The Origin of Silkworms

region.en: The silk country of the west (Sichuan–Shaanxi borders)

texts.period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 14

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 14: the girl of the old tale, the promised horse, and the wrapping of the silkworm

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A girl missed her father on a far journey and teased the family horse: bring him back and you shall have me. The horse broke its tether, carried the father home, and — remembered the promise — would not eat; the father killed and flayed it, drying the hide in the yard. The hide rolled itself up, swept the girl from the courtyard, and flew away with her to the mulberry trees, where both were found as a white silkworm wrapt in horse-hide — the origin of silkworms, and of the silkworm-princess worshipped in the sericulture lands.
summary.zh: 舊說太古之時，女念父不歸，戲語馬曰『汝得迎父，吾嫁汝』；馬絕韁迎父歸，不肯食；父殺之曝皮；皮忽卷女飛去，棲於桑樹之間——化為蠶，食桑葉，吐絲成繭——蠶神馬頭娘之由來。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original. Aition of sericulture and of the 'horse-head lady' (matou niang) silkworm goddess.

passages.text: In the oldest times, so the tale runs, a girl alone at home missed her father gone on a long journey, and teased the house's horse: 'If you bring him back, I will marry you.' The horse broke its tether that day, ran the roads until it found the father, and carried him home on its back — and thereafter would eat nothing, stamping and rearing whenever it saw the girl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 14, silkworm-girl episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The father asked the reason, learned the promise, and said a match between man and horse could not be; he shot the horse dead in the yard and had the hide spread out to dry. One day the girl walked over the hide — and the hide rolled itself up and swallowed her, and flew off with her into the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 14, the hide; not verbatim.

passages.text: The father searched for days, and found daughter and hide at last in the mulberry trees above the house — for there the pair had changed into a creature like a silkworm, eating mulberry leaves and spinning silk from itself. The sericulture lands built shrines to the girl as the Silkworm Princess, and the mulberry trees of the silk country are said to grow thickest where she was wrapt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 14, the silkworm and the cult; not verbatim.

title.en: Song Dingbo Catches a Ghost and Sells It

texts.period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 16 (also in Lieyichuan)

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 16: the night walk, the questions of the ghost, and the ghost spat into a market sale

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Walking to market by night, Song Dingbo met a ghost and, told what it was, answered that he was a ghost too. They carried each other by turns; the ghost, heavy as a man made of nothing, taught him its one weakness — human saliva. At the market crossing the ghost turned a goat; Song spat on it, held it, and sold it in the morning for fifteen hundred cash — the merchant's saying ever after: 'Song Dingbo sold a ghost for fifteen hundred.'
summary.zh: 宋定伯夜行逢鬼，問曰『汝復誰』——『我亦鬼』；鬼言唯不喜人唾；共遞相擔，至宛市，鬼化為羊，定伯唾之，賣得錢千五百——『定伯賣鬼，得錢千五百』。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original.

passages.text: Song Dingbo, a man of Nanyang, walked to market by night and met a figure on the road. 'Who goes?' said the figure. 'I am a ghost too,' said Song, coolly; and the two walked on together, the ghost asking what weighed so heavily on Song's shoulders — 'newly dead,' said Song, 'nothing is light for me yet.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 16, Song Dingbo episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: They carried each other by turns across the streams; the ghost, borne by Song, was light as a leaf. Song asked what ghosts feared; the ghost answered: 'Only the saliva of living men.' At the ford of the river the ghost bade Song cross silently; Song plunged through with a splash and said he was newly dead and knew no better.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 16, the ferrying; not verbatim.

passages.text: As the sky lightened at the market-gate, the ghost turned into a goat and tried to run; Song spat on it and held it fast, and sold it in the morning market for fifteen hundred cash. The merchants of Nanyang told the tale ever after as a price-list: 'Song Dingbo sold a ghost for fifteen hundred.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 16, the sale; not verbatim.

title.en: Liu Yi Delivers a Letter to the Dragon Palace of Dongting

region.en: Dongting Lake and the Jing River (Hunan–Shaanxi)

texts.period: Taiping Guangji, juan 419, from Li Chaowei's chuanqi 'Liuyi Zhuan' (Tang, c. 794 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 419: Liu Yi's letter-bearing, the sheep-herding lady on the Jing River, and the fire of the Qiantang dragon

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A failed examinee, Liu Yi, met a girl herding sheep on the Jing River who wept that she was the daughter of the Dragon King of Dongting, married off and abused by her husband's house; she gave him a letter, and told him to strike a tree by Dongting. In the Crystal Palace the wrathful younger brother, the Qiantang dragon, burst from the water as a red dragon a thousand feet long, ate the offending husband, and brought the lady home; Liu Yi refused a marriage of gratitude, and only years later — after a wife who died, a fisher of Wuzhou who was the lady in disguise — wed her as she truly was, a dragon-daughter immortal, and rose with her into the clouds.
summary.zh: 柳毅下第，涇陽遇牧羊龍女託書；至洞庭擊橘社树，龍宮震動；錢塘君怒誅涇川次子，救侄女歸；毅拒婚，後娶盧氏（即龍女所化），同登仙籍——傳書之報。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: Liu Yi, failing the examination, passed the Jing River and saw a girl herding a flock that were not sheep but water-thunder in sheep's shape; she wept that she was the daughter of the Dragon King of Dongting, married into the Jing River's house and beaten by its lord, and begged him to carry a letter — strike the tree of the orange-terrace by Dongting, and a messenger will come.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 419, Liuyi Zhuan (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Dongting he struck the tree thrice, and the lake opened into a corridor of water-walls, and servants of the Dragon King led him to the Crystal Palace. When the letter was read, a wail rose through the palace — and from the sky burst the Qiantang dragon, the wrathful younger brother, a red thunder a thousand feet tall, who seized the offending husband of the Jing River and ate him, then carried his niece home in triumph.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 419, the Qiantang dragon; not verbatim.

passages.text: The palace feasted him and offered the lady in marriage out of gratitude; Liu Yi, proud, refused and went home. Years later, his wife dead, he married a fisher-woman of Wuzhou who grew rich and mysterious — and at last she told him she was the dragon-daughter, who had not forgotten the man who carried her letter; they rose together into the clouds and were seen no more among the people of Dongting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 419, the marriage and the ascent; not verbatim.

title.en: The Dream of Nanke: A Career in an Ant Kingdom

texts.period: Taiping Guangji, juan 475, from Li Gongzuo's chuanqi 'Nanke Taishou Zhuan' (Tang, c. 813 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 475: Chunyu Fen's dream of the Great Locust Kingdom, his twenty years as governor, and the digging of the tree

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Chunyu Fen, drunk under a great locust tree, was carried off in a gilded carriage to a kingdom in the tree's hollow: he married the king's daughter, governed Nanke for twenty years, raised children, knew honor and disgrace — and woke at dusk under the same tree. Digging beneath it, his friends found an ant-city of perfect order in the hollow of the trunk, and a second colony to the west: Nanke, the kingdom of his career, one afternoon's dream in the life of a mound of ants.
summary.zh: 淳于棼夢入大槐安國，尚公主，守南柯郡二十年；夢醒，與客掘樹——樹下一蟻國，枝下一南柯郡——人生如蟻國一夢。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: Chunyu Fen sat drinking under the great locust tree of his garden and fell asleep; two purple-clad envoys carried him in a gilded carriage through a hole in the trunk into a kingdom whose gates bore the name Great Locust Ancestral Peace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 475, Nanke Taishou Zhuan (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king married him to his golden-braided daughter, posted him as governor of Nanke, and he reigned twenty years of the dream: good harvests, honors, sons and daughters, then disgrace and exile by the king's displeasure. The dream kingdom packed him back through the same hole in the trunk as dawn was near, and he woke in the dusk of his own garden with the wine-cups still unwashed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 475, the reign and the waking; not verbatim.

passages.text: His friends dug under the locust tree and found in the hollow a city of ants in perfect order — palaces, gates, guards — and beneath the western branch a second smaller colony: the Nanke of the dream. A storm that night scattered both cities to the winds; Chunyu Fen took vows and did not drink again under that tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 475, the ant-city; not verbatim.

title.en: The Yellow Millet Dream on the Handan Road

texts.period: Taiping Guangji, juan 82, from Shen Jiji's chuanqi 'Zhenzhong Ji' (Tang, c. 750 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 82: the pillow of Lü Weng, the millet still cooking, and the whole life of Lu Sheng

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A young man at the Handan post-house, lamenting his poverty to a Taoist with a magic pillow, fell asleep as the millet was set to cook: he lived in the dream a whole career — the brilliant marriage, the examination, the governorships, the wars, the chancellorship, the slanders, the exile, the old age — and died in the dream among his grandchildren. He woke, and the millet was not yet done; the Taoist smiled, and the young man bowed and went home having seen what a life is.
summary.zh: 呂翁於邯鄲道遇盧生，授青瓷枕——夢中娶崔氏、登第、陝州鑿河、大破吐蕃、拜相、遭讒、流放、復起、壽終——炊黃粱未熟。盧生悟，作禮而去。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: At the post-house of Handan a young man named Lu lamented to a Taoist traveler that he was born to nothing: talent without opportunity, poverty without end. The Taoist drew from his bag a pillow of green porcelain and said: 'Sleep on this; you will find in it all that you desire.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 82, Zhenzhong Ji (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Lu slept, and in the dream lived seventy years: he married the daughter of a great house, passed the examinations, governed provinces, drained the Yellow River's flood for the land's good, broke a Tibetan invasion, became grand chancellor — was slandered, exiled, recalled, honored — raised sons, married daughters, and died old and full of days in his bed among his grandchildren.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 82, the life in the dream; not verbatim.

passages.text: He woke on the post-house bench: the Taoist sat beside him, and the innkeeper's millet on the stove was not yet done cooking. Lu sat up a long time and then bowed: 'Glory and poverty, favor and loss, death and life — I have seen them all. Sir, you have quieted the passions of my heart.' He bowed again and went home, and the Yellow Millet Dream passed into the language of China as the name of every ambition seen whole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 82, the waking; not verbatim.

title.en: The Three-Lives Stone: Yuan Ze and Li Yuan

region.en: Tiantai Mountain and the Tianzhu Temple at Hangzhou

texts.period: Ganze Yao (Tang, c. 800 CE), 'Yuan Guan'; reprinted in the Taiping Guangji collections

source.work: Ganze Yao: Yuan Ze and Li Yuan's pact, the rebirth at the well of Tianzhu, and the Twelve-year meeting at the Three-Lives Stone

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Li Yuan, a retired general, and the monk Yuan Ze traveled toward Mount Emei; at a stream the monk saw a pregnant woman washing and went pale: his rebirth waited there. He asked Li Yuan to sing a song at the birth three days later, and to find him in twelve years at the Tianzhu temple of Hangzhou. Yuan Ze died, the child was born and spoke; twelve years on, Li Yuan came to Hangzhou, and a herd-boy by the Three-Lives Stone sang the promised song: 'the old soul on the third-life stone' — and was gone over the hills.
summary.zh: 李源與圓觀（一作圓澤）同遊；至江峽見妊婦汲水，觀曰『我託生之所』——約三日後浴兒相見、十二年後天竺寺相尋；圓觀坐化，兒生而能言；十二年李源至杭州天竺寺，牧童扣牛角歌曰『三生石上舊精魂』——遂杳然而去。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Ganze Yao text.

passages.text: Li Yuan, a general grown old in retreat, and his friend the monk Yuan Ze set out together for the mountains of the west; at a stream near the gorges Yuan Ze stopped, went pale at sight of a woman washing at the water, and said to Li Yuan: 'My rebirth waits in that house. I have put off going until now, but no one goes past it twice.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ganze Yao, Yuan Guan episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: He asked a last favor: come to the house in three days, and if the newborn smiles at you, that smile is mine; then find me in twelve years at the Tianzhu temple of Hangzhou, by the Three-Lives Stone. He bathed, sat upright, and died — and the child was born that night, and smiled at Li Yuan when he came.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ganze Yao, Yuan Guan episode, the pact; not verbatim.

passages.text: Twelve years later Li Yuan came to Hangzhou, and by the Three-Lives Stone of the Tianzhu temple a herd-boy sat on an ox, singing the very song Yuan Ze had promised: 'The old soul on the third-life stone; I do not regret the moon-song or the wind; my shame is only to meet you again, yet be a stranger going and coming.' He bowed across the distance, and was gone into the mists of the hill — friendship surviving death, by appointment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ganze Yao, Yuan Guan episode, the meeting; not verbatim.

title.en: The White Snake and the Leifeng Pagoda

region.en: West Lake and Leifeng Pagoda, Hangzhou

texts.period: Jingshi Tongyan by Feng Menglong, 1624 CE, juan 28

source.work: Jingshi Tongyan, juan 28: the white snake of West Lake, the umbrella at the broken bridge, the red-swallowing? truth, and the pagoda

texts.license: Public domain (Ming collection; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: At the Broken Bridge of West Lake a white snake in woman's form sheltered a young pharmacy clerk Xu Xian with his umbrella, married him, and made his fortune with her silver — silver that had been stolen, so that he was twice exiled for her sake. A Taoist tried to exorcise her, a monk Fahai of Jinshan pursued her: the white snake flooded the temple with the water of the whole lake, was captured, and sealed under the Leifeng Pagoda to wait a thousand years — the great love-story of the snake and the man, told by Feng Menglong as a warning, loved by the people as a tragedy.
summary.zh: 西湖斷橋白蛇借傘許仙，成親開藥鋪；銀兩皆來路不明，許仙兩度充軍；道士除妖不成，金山寺法海鬥法水漫金山；白娘子被缽收，鎮於雷峰塔下——『雷峰塔倒，白蛇出世』。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Feng Menglong text.

passages.text: At the Broken Bridge of West Lake, in the rain, a woman in white and her green-robed maid sheltered a young clerk of the medicine shops and lent him an umbrella; he called for it next day, drank tea, and before the month was out the white-clad lady was his wife, her dowry of fifty taels of silver furnishing the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jingshi Tongyan, juan 28 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The silver was traced: it had been stolen from an official's house, and Xu Xian was arrested twice for goods that appeared from nowhere. The truth was worse than theft: his wife was a white snake of a thousand years' cultivation, her maid a green snake, and a wandering Taoist who tried to hang a charm on the marriage was driven off with a strip of her serpent's tail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jingshi Tongyan, juan 28, the truth; not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the monk Fahai of Jinshan temple took the case. When the white snake flooded his temple with the whole of West Lake to rescue her husband, he brought forth the alms-bowl of the Buddha: she was caught in it, sealed with the Leifeng Pagoda built over her on the lake shore, and told she would wait under it a thousand years — until the pagoda falls, said the storytellers, and the white snake comes out again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jingshi Tongyan, juan 28, the pagoda; not verbatim.

title.en: Xiao Shi and Nong Yu: The Flute That Called the Phoenixes

region.en: Phoenix Terrace, the palace of Duke Mu of Qin (Shaanxi)

texts.period: Liexian Zhuan (Biographies of Immortals), attributed Liu Xiang, Han dynasty

source.work: Liexian Zhuan: Xiao Shi the flute-player, the duke's daughter Nong Yu, and the phoenixes of the terrace

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Duke Mu of Qin had a daughter, Nong Yu, who loved the pan-pipes; a young man called Xiao Shi played the xiao flute so that peacocks and phoenixes gathered on his roof. He married the princess and taught her; they lived half a life above the terrace they were given, and one morning, playing, they called down the phoenix and the dragon — she rode the phoenix, he rode the dragon, and both rose together into the sky, leaving the Qin court a tower and a lesson: music, sincerely practiced, is the road of the immortals.
summary.zh: 蕭史善簫，能致孔雀白鶴；穆公以女弄玉妻之；居鳳樓數年，一朝隨鳳凰昇天——秦作鳳女祠，簫聲之仙由此立。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Liexian Zhuan text.

passages.text: Xiao Shi of the Qin lands played the xiao so that its notes drew the cries of peacocks and the songs of white cranes; the Duke Mu heard of it, married him to his daughter Nong Yu, who was herself a master of the pan-pipes, and gave the pair a tower of their own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liexian Zhuan, Xiao Shi biography (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: For several years the two played together on the tower morning and night, until their music called down the phoenixes themselves: great birds settled on the tower's roof, and the duke built a terrace of phoenix and named the city's gate for them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liexian Zhuan, Xiao Shi biography, the phoenixes; not verbatim.

passages.text: One morning the flute called a pair down for the last time: Nong Yu mounted the phoenix, Xiao Shi the dragon that came with it, and husband and wife rose together into the sky, never to be seen in Qin again — leaving the duke a terrace, a shrine, and the teaching that the flute of the immortals is played by two.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liexian Zhuan, Xiao Shi biography, the ascent; not verbatim.
